steps.text: The exponential function is the most important function in analysis: it describes growth and decay, solves differential equations and appears constantly in probability, physics and computer science. Here you get to know it as a function – together with its inverse, the logarithm.
steps.explanation:
Our roadmap:
1. The function \(a^x\) and its growth behaviour
2. Why the number \(e\) is so special
3. The natural logarithm as the inverse function
4. Growth, decay, saturation
steps.insight: Hallmark of exponential growth: in each equal time step the quantity is multiplied by the same factor – not increased by the same amount.

steps.text: For a base \(a > 0\), \(f(x) = a^x\) is defined for ALL real \(x\) – not only for integers (via \(a^{p/q} = \sqrt[q]{a^p}\) and limits).
steps.explanation:
Properties for \(a > 0\), \(a \neq 1\):
• Domain \(\mathbb{R}\), range \((0, \infty)\): the value is always positive.
• All graphs pass through \((0, 1)\), since \(a^0 = 1\).
• For \(a > 1\): strictly increasing (growth). For \(0 < a < 1\): strictly decreasing (decay).
• Power laws: \(a^{x+y} = a^x \cdot a^y\), \((a^x)^y = a^{xy}\).

Each step of \(1\) to the right multiplies the value by \(a\). For \(2^x\) it doubles, for \((\frac{1}{2})^x\) it halves.
steps.insight: The exponential function has no root: \(a^x > 0\) for all \(x\). The \(x\)-axis is a horizontal asymptote.

steps.text: Percentage growth is exponential: if a quantity grows by \(p\,\%\) per year, it is multiplied each year by the factor \(1 + \frac{p}{100}\).
steps.formula: N(t) = N_0 \cdot a^t, \qquad N(t) = N_0 \cdot \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T} \ \text{(half-life } T)
steps.explanation:
Examples:
• \(\text{€}200\) at \(3\,\%\) interest: \(N(t) = 200 \cdot 1.03^t\). After \(5\) years: \(200 \cdot 1.03^5 \approx \text{€}231.85\).
• A substance with half-life \(T = 5\) years: after \(t\) years \((\frac{1}{2})^{t/5}\) remains. After \(10\) years \(\frac{1}{4}\), after \(15\) years \(\frac{1}{8}\).

Linear growth is different: a fixed amount is added each year. In the long run exponential growth beats every linear function.
steps.insight: Factor \(> 1\): growth. Factor between \(0\) and \(1\): decay. A decrease by \(p\,\%\) means the factor \(1 - \frac{p}{100}\).

steps.text: Which base is "the natural one"? If you look at the slope of the tangent to \(a^x\) at the point \((0, 1)\), it depends on \(a\). Euler's number \(e\) is exactly the base for which the slope is \(1\).
steps.explanation:
The animation shows the tangents at \(x = 0\):
• \(2^x\): slope \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69\) – flatter than \(45°\).
• \(3^x\): slope \(\ln 3 \approx 1.10\) – steeper.
• \(e^x\): slope exactly \(1\).

That's why \(e^x\) is the only function equal to its own derivative – which makes it the standard for growth and differential equations.

\(e\) can be understood as a limit of the compound-interest formula: at \(100\,\%\) interest compounded \(n\) times a year, \(\text{€}1\) grows to \((1 + \frac{1}{n})^n\): \(n = 1\): \(2\), \(n = 12\): \(2.613\), \(n = 365\): \(2.7146\), \(n \to \infty\): \(e\).
steps.insight: Remember: \((e^x)' = e^x\). This is no coincidence but the very reason to introduce \(e\).

steps.text: Every exponential function can be written with base \(e\). That is the standard in analysis.
steps.explanation:
Reason: \(a = e^{\ln a}\), so \(a^x = (e^{\ln a})^x = e^{x \ln a}\) – power of a power.

Concretely: \(N(t) = 100 \cdot 1.03^t = 100 \cdot e^{kt}\) with \(k = \ln 1.03 \approx 0.0296\).

\(k > 0\): growth rate, \(k < 0\): decay rate. Advantage of the \(e\) notation: the rate \(k\) stands directly in the exponent, and differentiating is easy: \((e^{kt})' = k\,e^{kt}\).

Rules: \(e^{x + y} = e^x \cdot e^y\), \(e^{-x} = \frac{1}{e^x}\), \((e^x)^y = e^{xy}\).
steps.insight: All exponential functions are "disguised" \(e\)-functions: only the rate \(k = \ln a\) distinguishes them.

steps.text: The natural logarithm \(\ln\) is the inverse function of \(e^x\). It answers: "To which power must I raise \(e\) to get \(x\)?"
steps.explanation:
Properties of \(\ln\):
• Domain \((0, \infty)\), range \(\mathbb{R}\).
• Strictly increasing, root at \(x = 1\).
• \(\ln x < 0\) for \(0 < x < 1\), \(\ln x > 0\) for \(x > 1\).
• The graph is the graph of \(e^x\) reflected in \(y = x\).

Rules (see "Powers, Roots & Logarithms"): \(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\), \(\ln\frac{a}{b} = \ln a - \ln b\), \(\ln(a^r) = r \ln a\).

Values worth knowing: \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\), \(\ln 10 \approx 2.303\), \(\ln e^3 = 3\), \(\ln\frac{1}{e} = -1\).
steps.insight: The logarithm grows extremely slowly: \(\ln 1000 \approx 6.9\), \(\ln 10^6 \approx 13.8\). That makes it the scale for huge ranges.

steps.text: How fast do \(e^x\) and \(\ln x\) grow compared with powers? This later decides many limits.
steps.explanation:
• \(e^x\) grows faster than every power \(x^n\) for \(x \to \infty\), no matter how large \(n\) is. Example: \(x = 10\): \(e^{10} \approx 22\,026\), but \(10^3 = 1000\).
• \(\ln x\) grows more slowly than every root \(\sqrt[n]{x}\).
• For \(x \to -\infty\): \(e^x \to 0\), so \(e^{-x}\) for \(x \to \infty\) falls towards \(0\) (decay).
• For \(x \to 0^+\): \(\ln x \to -\infty\).

Careful: over short stretches \(x^3\) can exceed \(e^x\) – at \(x = 3\), \(x^3 = 27 > e^3 \approx 20.1\). Only for large \(x\) does \(e^x\) win for good.
steps.insight: Rule of thumb for limits: "exponential beats polynomial beats logarithmic."

steps.text: With the \(e\) notation, growth and decay can be described uniformly: \(N(t) = N_0 \cdot e^{kt}\).
steps.explanation:
Derivation of the doubling time: \(N_0 e^{kT} = 2N_0 \Rightarrow e^{kT} = 2 \Rightarrow kT = \ln 2\).

Example: growth rate \(k = 0.05\) per year: \(T_2 = \frac{0.693}{0.05} \approx 13.9\) years – independent of the initial value.

Example C-14: half-life \(5730\) years, so \(\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{5730} \approx 1.21 \cdot 10^{-4}\) per year. A find with \(25\,\%\) of the original C-14 is \(2 \cdot 5730 = 11\,460\) years old.

Times we're looking for are in the exponent – hence we need the logarithm: \(60\,\%\) remaining: \(e^{-\lambda t} = 0.6 \Rightarrow t = \frac{\ln(1/0.6)}{\lambda} \approx 4223\) years.
steps.insight: Doubling time and half-life depend only on the rate, not on the amount. That is the hallmark of exponential processes.

steps.text: Compound interest and continuous compounding: what happens when interest is paid more and more often?
steps.explanation:
Annual compounding at \(4\,\%\) for \(10\) years: \(1000 \cdot 1.04^{10} = \text{€}1480.24\).

Continuous compounding at the same rate: \(1000 \cdot e^{0.4} = \text{€}1491.82\). This is the limit of the formula \((1 + \frac{r}{n})^n \to e^r\) as compounding becomes ever more frequent.

The difference is only \(\text{€}11.58\): more frequent compounding helps a little, but not without bound – there is a limit.

Connection: the effective annual rate of continuous compounding is \(e^{0.04} - 1 \approx 4.08\,\%\).
steps.insight: The limit \(\lim (1 + \frac{r}{n})^n = e^r\) is the reason \(e\) appears in financial mathematics and probability.

steps.text: Not all growth is unlimited. Bounded growth and cooling approach a limit – also with \(e\)-functions.
steps.formula: T(t) = T_A + (T_0 - T_A)\, e^{-kt}, \qquad S(t) = S \cdot \left(1 - e^{-kt}\right)
steps.explanation:
Newton's law of cooling: a coffee (\(T_0 = 90\,°\text{C}\)) in a room at \(T_A = 20\,°\text{C}\) cools with \(k = 0.1\) per minute:
\(T(t) = 20 + 70\,e^{-0.1 t}\).
• After \(10\) minutes: \(20 + 70 \cdot e^{-1} \approx 45.75\,°\text{C}\).
• For \(t \to \infty\), \(T\) approaches room temperature \(20\,°\text{C}\) – but never reaches it.
• When is the coffee \(40\,°\text{C}\)? \(70 e^{-0.1 t} = 20 \Rightarrow t = 10 \ln 3.5 \approx 12.5\) minutes.

For saturation growth \(S(t) = S(1 - e^{-kt})\) you start at \(0\) and approach the maximum \(S\) from below.
steps.insight: The factor \(e^{-kt}\) tends to \(0\): it switches off the deviation from the limit exponentially.

steps.text: Logarithmic scales make huge ranges manageable: each step multiplies by the same factor, but the scale rises by a fixed number.
steps.explanation:
• Magnitude \(+1\) means \(10\) times the amplitude. An earthquake of magnitude \(7\) has \(100\) times the amplitude of one of magnitude \(5\), since \(10^{7-5} = 100\).
• \(+3\) dB means roughly twice the intensity: \(10^{0.3} \approx 2\).
• pH \(7\) versus pH \(5\): \(100\) times lower concentration of \(\mathrm{H^+}\) ions.

Why? \(\lg(10^n) = n\): the logarithm turns powers of ten into exponents. Calculating with factors becomes calculating with sums.
steps.insight: On logarithmic scales exponential processes look like straight lines. This is used in growth charts.

steps.text: Look back at what you can do now:
steps.explanation:
1. \(a^x\): always positive, through \((0, 1)\); increasing for \(a > 1\), decreasing for \(0 < a < 1\). Percentage change = factor.

2. \(e \approx 2.718\): the base with tangent slope \(1\) at \(0\). \((e^x)' = e^x\). \(a^x = e^{x \ln a}\).

3. \(\ln\) is the inverse function of \(e^x\): \(D = (0, \infty)\), strictly increasing, \(\ln 1 = 0\).

4. \(e^x \gg x^n \gg \ln x\) for \(x \to \infty\).

5. \(N(t) = N_0 e^{kt}\): doubling time \(\frac{\ln 2}{k}\). Cooling and saturation approach a limit.
steps.insight: Congratulations! The exponential function and the logarithm return in full glory in "Differential Calculus" (derivatives), "Integral Calculus" (antiderivatives) and "Complex Numbers" (\(e^{i\varphi}\)).
